Whether fires benefit forests is a genuinely contested question, with the answer depending heavily on forest type, fire severity, and context. [d1] and [d3] strongly support the view that fires benefit many ecosystems: National Geographic notes that "many ecosystems benefit from periodic fires, because they clear out dead organic material—and some plant and animal populations require the benefits fire brings to survive and reproduce," while Natural Resources Canada states that "fire, the primary change agent in the boreal zone, is as crucial to forest renewal as the sun and rain," releasing nutrients, stimulating new growth, and enabling reproduction of species like lodgepole and jack pine. [d5] (Penn State) adds that in 83% of studies evaluated, spotted owls were not significantly affected by wildfire, and where effects existed they were mostly beneficial, with fires creating biodiverse "snag forests." [d2] and [d4] similarly describe how small fires create habitat, encourage biodiversity, kill diseases, and restore soil nutrients, though both acknowledge that fires also pose risks to air quality and human lives. In contrast, [d8] (WWF) and [d6] (Nature journal) present a strongly negative view: fires destroy or degrade millions of acres of forest annually, threaten biodiversity, alter water cycles and soil fertility, and in Indonesia the losses and damages from fires outweigh any savings from using fire as a land-clearing method. [d9] (BBC/Oxford) captures the core tension most directly, noting that "there is a case to be made that some fire-adapted forests benefit from fires," but that "the humid forests of the Amazon have no adaptation to fire and suffer immense damage," with almost all Amazon fires being human-caused. [d7] (UN) frames fires primarily as a threat to forests rather than a benefit. In summary, the evidence shows that periodic, natural fires can benefit fire-adapted forests (boreal, temperate conifer), but fires in non-fire-adapted ecosystems like tropical rainforests, or large-scale human-caused fires, are broadly harmful.
